Abstract
Ethereum’s consensus safety relies on independent consensus client
implementations agreeing on every state transition. When they di-
verge due to implementation errors, the network can fork, finality
can stall, and severe attacks are possible. To prevent such consensus
divergences , Ethereum provides a Python reference implementation
( consensus-spec ), which acts as a specification, and a hand-crafted
official test suite ( spectests ). However, as an executable implemen-
tation, Ethereum’s specification defines validity implicitly through
runtime behavior. As a result, it lacks a systematic way to ensure
that all validity conditions are thoroughly evaluated.
We present SpecTrum, a framework that addresses this problem
in three stages. First, we introduce Consensus-SpecTec, a mech-
anized specification of the Ethereum consensus algorithm, which
makes validity conditions explicit as if-premises . Second, we de-
fine premise coverage , a metric that measures which if-premises
are evaluated to true and false across spectests . Third, we develop
a specification-based test generator that extracts constraints on
premises not evaluated to false by spectests and generates inputs
to evaluate them. Applying SpecTrum to five major Ethereum con-
sensus clients, we identify 27 cross-client divergence cases, 22 of
which cannot be found without the premises inserted in our mecha-
nization. All 27 cases reproduce across fork versions, and extending
the mechanized specification to a new fork takes modest effort
proportional to the specification difference.

1 Introduction
Ethereum’s safety depends on independent consensus clients com-
puting the same state transition for the same pre-state and block.
Ethereum promotes client diversity to reduce the risk of single-
implementation failures [5]: major clients include Lighthouse
(Rust) [36], Lodestar (TypeScript) [9], Nimbus (Nim) [29], Prysm
(Go) [31], and Teku (Java) [15]. Diversity improves resilience, but
differences in how clients interpret the protocol can cause inconsis-
tent state-transition outcomes. Such inconsistencies may lead to
incorrect validator penalties, chain splits, or stalled finality, threat-
ening network reliability [30, 35, 38].
The primary conformance baseline is the official Ethereum con-
sensus specification, consensus-spec [16], together with the accom-
panying hand-written specification tests ( spectests ) [19], which
clients use to check conformance [1, 2, 4]. As executable Python,
consensus-spec is complete : every transition either produces a post-
state or raises an exception, as the specification states [18]:
State transitions that trigger an unhandled exception
(e.g. a failed assert or an out-of-range list access)
are considered invalid. State transitions that cause
a uint64 overflow or underflow are also considered
invalid.
This convention, however, defines invalidity only through run-
time behavior, rather than as explicit conditions. In addition, the
checks are scattered across overlapping conditional statements and
in-place state mutations. A developer porting consensus-spec to
other languages must recover these conditions from the code, not
from a list of validity rules. We call such conditions implicit : not ab-
sent or ambiguous, but hidden behind implementation details such
as mutation, condition fallthrough, or runtime exceptions. Such
symptoms are not unique to Ethereum: specifications are often
given as reference implementations that encode validity implicitly.
As we show in §7.2, this implicitness hides these conditions from
code-level coverage, and leads to under-testing. This is a significant

limitation, because consensus bugs arise from such validity condi-
tions, particularly boundary cases [23, 35, 38]. Existing differential
fuzzers [25, 28, 35, 38] cannot sufficiently cover such boundaries,
because they select mutation targets without reference to the spec-
ification’s validity conditions.
We address this problem with SpecTrum, a specification-guided
differential testing framework for Ethereum consensus clients. The
key component of SpecTrum is Consensus-SpecTec, a mechanized
specification of the Ethereum consensus algorithm. It explicitly
specifies the mutation semantics, branching structure, and implicit
exception boundaries as if-premises . On top of this mechanized
specification, we define premise coverage , a structural coverage
metric that measures whether each failure-relevant premise is eval-
uated to both true and false. Because these conditions are now
explicit, premise coverage finds validity conditions that spectests
under-executes and code-level coverage cannot see. SpecTrum uses
spectests as seeds, tracks how input values (e.g., states) are de-
rived during execution, extracts constraints from under-executed
premises, and generates tests that execute those premises or target
their boundary values. The generated tests are executed across
independent clients, and disagreements in outcome or post-state
are reported as divergences.
Our evaluation shows that SpecTrum is both effective and practi-
cal. We first validate Consensus-SpecTec against 910 official tests,
including 581 state-transition tests and 329 unit tests, and obtain full
agreement with consensus-spec . We then apply SpecTrum to the
five major Ethereum consensus clients and identify 27 cross-client
divergences across six root-cause categories, leading to consensus
failures, liveness failures, and client crashes. Some divergences are
silent: clients accept the same input yet compute different post-
states, undetectable by accept/reject testing. We have reported all
the identified divergences to the Ethereum Protocol Bug Bounty
Program ( bounty@ethereum.org ) and they are awaiting triage.
The technical contributions of this paper include the following:
• Consensus-SpecTec , a mechanized specification of the
Ethereum consensus algorithm, which makes consensus-
spec ’s implicit validity conditions explicit as if-premises. It
is the first application of the SpecTec approach [26, 39] to
non-programming-language software.
• Premise coverage , a structural coverage metric defined
over if-premises, which identifies 151 conditions not covered
by spectests , 81 of which are inserted.
• A specification-guided test generator that traces in-
put provenance through Consensus-SpecTec, extracts con-
straints to cover the target conditions, and samples values,
raising premise coverage from 46.3% to 91.1%.
• A comprehensive empirical evaluation demonstrating
SpecTrum’s effectiveness and practicality through improved
premise coverage, 27 cross-client divergence cases across six
root-cause categories, superiority over unguided mutation,
and transfer across protocol forks.
2 Background
2.1 Ethereum State Transition
In Ethereum’s Proof-of-Stake protocol (Gasper [8]), validators are
network participants who stake ETH to propose and attest to blocks.

The protocol divides time into fixed-length slots , grouped into
epochs of 32 slots each. In each slot, one validator is chosen as
the proposer and submits a BeaconBlock , which packages new trans-
actions, attestations, and validator operations. All other validators
are attesters who validate the proposed block. Each validator runs
a consensus client : an implementation that handles consensus logic,
including block proposal, validation, and fork choice. These op-
erations update the BeaconState , a persistent data structure that
stores validator registries, balances, committee assignments, and
finalized checkpoints. States and blocks are serialized with SSZ,
the protocol’s encoding. Each consensus client 𝐶 implements the
state-transition function 𝑓 𝐶 , defined by the Ethereum consensus
specification. This function takes the current BeaconState 𝑆 and

First, process_slots advances the state slot-by-slot from its cur-
rent slot to the block’s target slot, applying per-slot ( process_slot )
and per-epoch ( process_epoch ) transitions at each step. Second,
process_block applies block-specific updates through a sequence of
sub-functions, each validating one aspect of the block and updating
the state.
The specification defines an additional validate_result flag (de-
fault True ) that controls whether the block signature and the post-
state root are checked against the values the block carries. Validators
selected as proposers set this flag to False during block construc-
tion to avoid a circular dependency [16], whereas attesters use True
when validating received blocks.

2.4 SpecTec
SpecTec [26, 39] is a mechanization framework for language spec-
ifications. It consists of a domain-specific language (DSL) and a
toolchain that generates interpreters, tests, and prose documents
from specifications written in the DSL. SpecTec was originally de-
signed to mechanize the WebAssembly (Wasm) specification [39],
and P4-SpecTec is a redesign of SpecTec centered on algorithmic
inference rules [26]. While this work uses P4-SpecTec, for the sake
of brevity, this paper refers to it simply as SpecTec.
Specifications written in the SpecTec DSL are organized as a
set of rules , each defining one case of a relation. The rule below
illustrates the syntax:
1 rule WeighJustification/justify_prev:
2 state total_bal prev_bal cur_bal ~> state[.CUR_JCP = prev_epoch]
3 -- if total_bal <= $UINT64_MAX / 2 ;; inserted: overflow
4 -- if prev_bal * 3 >= total_bal * 2
5 -- if ~(cur_bal * 3 >= total_bal * 2)
6 -- if prev_epoch = $get_prev_epoch(state)
Line 1 is the rule name. Line 2 is the conclusion : the relation instance
being defined, which updates the state’s CUR_JCP field. Lines 3–6
are the premises : the conditions that must hold for the conclu-
sion to apply. However, not all premises represent validity con-
ditions. Line 6 binds prev_epoch to the result of the function call
$get_prev_epoch(state) : it introduces a new name for the result of
a pure computation. The other premises are boolean conditions. If
the evaluation of a boolean condition yields false, the transition
becomes invalid. We refer to bindings of purely computational re-
sults as let-premises , and boolean conditions as if-premises . As we
present in §5, premise coverage is defined only over if-premises.
Finally, the comment on line 3 indicates that the premise has been
inserted. In other words, consensus-spec does not have a corre-
sponding condition; instead, it relies on an implicit exception when
total_bal * 2 overflows. We discuss this class of premise insertion
in §4.
3 Overview
Fig. 1 illustrates an overview of SpecTrum. The foundation of Spec-
Trum is Consensus-SpecTec (§4), the mechanized specification
of the Ethereum consensus algorithm in the SpecTec DSL. It makes
branch conditions and implicit exceptions explicit as if-premises.
From this, the SpecTec toolchain generates an executable inter-
preter, over which the remaining stages operate.
In the Premise Coverage (§5) stage, we collect seed inputs
from spectests , selecting tests that target the state_transition
function, and flatten multi-block sequences into individual ( 𝑆,𝐵 )
pairs. We then measure premise coverage : for each if-premise in
the mechanized specification, we record whether the seed suite
evaluates it to true, to false, or to both. We manually inspect the
never-falsified premises to exclude unfalsifiable conditions, yielding
the set of target premises.
In the Test Generation stage, the generator propagates prove-
nance from input fields to runtime values (§6.1), negates the condi-
tion of each target premise to identify which fields to mutate (§6.2),
and samples values from the resulting intervals (§6.3), producing
mutated ( 𝑆,𝐵 ) pairs.

4 Mechanized Specification
Consensus-SpecTec makes three aspects of consensus-spec ex-
plicit: mutation semantics, branching structure, and exception
boundaries. We demonstrate these aspects with a simplified version
of the function weigh_justification_and_finalization in Fig. 2a.
For illustration purposes, we show only the core justification logic,
whereas the original weigh_justification_and_finalization func-
tion additionally handles finalization.
Lines 4–5 and 6–7 are independent if-blocks—not if-else—that
both update cur_justified_cp . If both conditions hold, the second
silently overwrites the first. Because such if-blocks interact through
a shared state but are not connected by control flow, a branch-
coverage tool can execute each block’s true and false branches,
achieving 100% coverage, without testing specific combinations that
determine which checkpoints are justified. Also, the multiplication

5 Premise Coverage
For each if-premise, premise coverage tracks whether spectests
evaluate it to true or false. A premise is fully covered when it
is evaluated to both values. This metric is motivated by clause
coverage [7, 14], where each clause in a compound condition must
evaluate to both true and false. In the SpecTec DSL, the compound
condition of each rule is the conjunction of its if-premises, and each
if-premise is an individual clause.
Evaluating a premise to false is particularly informative because
an if-premise can play one of two roles, depending on the other
rules in the relation. If the premise appears identically across all
rules, such as the overflow checks on lines 3, 8, and 14 in Fig. 2b,
it acts as an assertion: failing it rejects the transition regardless of
which rule is applied. If the premise distinguishes one rule from
another, such as the justification condition on line 4, it acts as a
branch condition: failing it causes a different rule to be applied
(line 9). We target both roles in our test generation.

6 Test Generation and Differential Testing
The goal of the test generator is to produce inputs that falsify the
target premises identified by the coverage analysis of §5. Given a
seed input ( 𝑆,𝐵 ) that reaches a target premise 𝑝 and evaluates it
to true, the generator determines which fields of 𝑆 or 𝐵 to mutate
and what values to substitute so that 𝑝 evaluates to false. However,
input fields and premise operands are connected only indirectly:
values pass through helper functions, arithmetic operations, and
record constructions before reaching a premise.
To address this, the generator operates in three phases. Prove-
nance propagation (§6.1) tracks which input fields contribute to
each runtime value, suggestion extraction (§6.2) negates each target
premise’s constraint and pairs it with those fields, and mutation
application (§6.3) turns each suggestion into concrete substitutions.
Differential testing (§6.4) then executes the generated tests across
the clients and compares their outcomes.

gences. As shown in Table 3, Random exposes 12 divergence cases
and Extreme 16, whereas SpecTrum identifies 27. The Matched
column counts control cases corresponding to the same implemen-
tation fault and affected clients as a SpecTrum case (§7.1). Random
and Extreme match 7 and 11 of SpecTrum’s cases, respectively. The
two controls overlap only partially, and together they match only 12
of SpecTrum’s 27 cases. Under full validation, Random exposes no
Class-A divergence, whereas Extreme exposes four, three of which
match a SpecTrum case.
Control-Only Divergences. Each control exposes five divergence
cases not found by SpecTrum. Most arise from different seed se-
lection: SpecTrum selects 59 seeds to maximize premise coverage,
whereas the controls sample uniformly from all 581 state-transition
seeds. A larger seed budget would likely recover these cases (§7.5).
One case in each control targets a premise already falsified by the
baseline spectests , which SpecTrum intentionally excludes from its
target set. The remaining Extreme case mutates block.state_root ,
which is unchecked under validate_result=False . Also, two inputs
excluded from the counts in Table 3 expose disagreements between
consensus-spec and all five clients while the clients agree with
one another. These disagreements arise from an optimization in
consensus-spec that the clients do not implement and are therefore
not considered cross-client divergences.
Premise Coverage. Premise coverage measures which condi-
tions a test suite exercises, rather than which faults it exposes.
SpecTrum falsifies 126 additional premises beyond the baseline
spectests , about twice as many as Extreme (57) and Random (63).
Though the metric favors SpecTrum by construction, it also shows
that the implicit conditions are difficult to cover without specifica-
tion guidance. Interestingly, Random falsifies more premises than
Extreme , yet exposes fewer divergences and no consensus failures.
Mutation Strategy and Field Selection. Both mutation strat-
egy and field selection contribute to SpecTrum’s advantage. The
controls differ only in mutation strategy, which accounts for four
additional divergence cases and all Class-A cases found by Extreme .
The remaining gap is due to field selection: without specification
guidance, a generator chooses among all 145 field paths (65 in
BeaconState and 80 in BeaconBlock ), whereas premise coverage and
provenance tracking identify the fields that affect state validity.
7.4 RQ4: Cross-Fork Bug Reproducibility and
Maintainability
Bugs in shared logic affect all fork versions that inherit the af-
fected functions [16]. Clients support every fork version within a
single codebase, and much of the state-transition logic is shared
across forks. The specification maintainers apply fixes, terminology
changes, and refactors across all fork versions simultaneously [37],
indicating that all versions remain actively maintained. We evaluate
whether the divergences identified under the Capella configuration
(RQ1) also manifest under the Deneb configuration, using the same
specification and client versions.
Extending Consensus-SpecTec from Capella to Deneb changes
+26 lines (about 1%) across 10 of 22 specification files. The
Seokhun Jeong, Gyeongmin Dan, Sukyoung Ryu, and Sungjae Hwang
changes are local to constants, type definitions, container struc-
tures, and fork-specific block-processing functions. The premise
count changes correspondingly, from 392 to 388: Deneb relaxes the
attestation-inclusion bound, removing five premises, and adds one
bound on blob commitments. After adjusting the target premises
(§5), the remaining pipeline applies without modification, generat-
ing 21,825 valid SSZ test cases for the Deneb configuration. Premise
coverage transfers as well. Under the same classification (§5), the
baseline spectests falsify 131 of 280 falsifiable if-premises, and the
combined suite 261 (93.2%), a gain of 130 matching Capella’s 126.
All 27 divergence cases from RQ1 reproduce identically under
the Deneb configuration. Each client produces the same outcome
(acceptance, rejection, or crash) on the corresponding Deneb-format
input as it did on the Capella-format input. All six root causes reside
in functions that Deneb inherits unchanged from Capella.
Due to the incremental structure of the specification, if a bug
exists in the shared logic, it appears in all fork versions that include
it. All 27 cases confirm this. Each case originated in a shared func-
tion and is reproducible in both tested fork versions. Because the
mechanization also targets shared logic, a one-time effort on the
specification core extends to all fork versions that inherit it. The
+26-line difference required to extend Consensus-SpecTec from
Capella to Deneb demonstrates that the required effort is modest
and proportional to the specification differences.
7.5 Discussion
Seeds and Mutation Breadth. Two factors currently limit the
input space explored by SpecTrum. The first is the seed pool. A
valid BeaconState must satisfy complex cryptographic constraints,
including hash value comparisons across fields, so SpecTrum mu-
tates spectests inputs instead of synthesizing pairs from scratch.
Then, each target premise is executed by at most seven pre-states
in our evaluation. As shown in §7.3, additional pre-states expose
further divergence cases, suggesting that a larger seed budget could
improve bug-finding ability. The second is single-field mutation.
Premises whose falsification requires coordinated changes to multi-
ple fields cannot be targeted this way, and reaching them requires
multi-field mutation.
Manual Effort. The mechanization is a one-time engineering ef-
fort. Consensus-SpecTec comprises 2,632 lines and 392 if-premises,
written over roughly three months by a developer new to the
SpecTec DSL. Once completed, all subsequent stages are automatic.
Maintenance is modest because Ethereum specifications evolve
incrementally across forks. For example, extending Consensus-
SpecTec from Capella to Deneb required only 26 changed lines
(§7.4). Classifying the 392 if-premises into 56 tautologies, 55 closing
branches, and 281 falsifiable premises (§5) took roughly two days.
The process is largely mechanical, and could be partly automated
with structural checks and SMT-based tautology detection for a
larger specification. An error in this classification is also bounded
in consequence, because Consensus-SpecTec guides generation
rather than deciding correctness (§6.4).
Non-Target Premise Classification. Excluding non-targets is
conservative. Misclassifying a target premise as a non-target only
makes the generator skip a valid target, which may reduce coverage
but does not produce false positives.

Generality. Once the mechanization is in place, the rest of the
pipeline is domain-agnostic. It applies to any domain with several
independent implementations of a specification whose validity is
left implicit.
7.6 Threats to Validity
Internal Validity. Our evaluation relies on two reference artifacts:
consensus-spec for fault attribution and Consensus-SpecTec for
test generation. If consensus-spec is incorrect, fault attribution
may be affected. Such errors would appear as inputs on which
consensus-spec alone disagrees with all clients. Our controls ex-
posed two such cases (§7.3), both caused by an optimization in
consensus-spec rather than client faults. Faults shared by consensus-
spec and a subset of clients would not be detected in this way. For
Consensus-SpecTec, incorrect premises may direct test generation
toward unintended boundaries. We mitigate this threat by deriving
premises directly from consensus-spec and validating the generated
interpreter against all 910 official reference tests.
Construct Validity. Branch coverage tools vary in capability
across the five implementation languages, which may affect ab-
solute coverage values. The go-bcov tool we use for Prysm may
miss short-circuit evaluation, and Nimbus’s branch denominator
includes build artifacts due to limited gcov support for Nim. These
differences affect cross-client comparisons, but for each client, the
baseline and combined suites use identical instrumentation.
External Validity. We evaluate SpecTrum on one protocol version
(Capella) with cross-fork reproduction on Deneb. The specification
defines seven fork versions. While RQ4 shows that bugs in the
shared logic reproduce across forks, SpecTrum targets the state-
transition function and does not cover fork-choice rules, light-client
protocols, or the execution layer. We test the five major actively
maintained clients, excluding minor and experimental ones.
8 Related Work
Specification-Guided Testing. JEST [32] mechanizes the EC-
MAScript specification and generates JavaScript programs to differ-
entially test browser engines. WEST [40] generates Wasm programs
from a mechanized Wasm specification using the SpecTec [39]
toolchain. Closest to our work, Lee et al. [27] mechanize the P4 type
system in P4-SpecTec, define dangling coverage over the premises
whose violation makes a program ill-typed, and mutate well-typed
seed programs to cover them. RFCcert [10] extracts validation rules
from RFC prose and assembles certificates by dynamic symbolic
execution. All four operate on specifications that state which inputs
are valid, in the form of ECMAScript early errors, Wasm validation
rules, P4 typing rules, and X.509 certificate requirements. Since
consensus-spec does not specify validation conditions and these
conditions exist solely as Python control flow, SpecTrum recovers
them as if-premises, enabling the definition of premise coverage.
Differential Fuzzing for Blockchain Consensus. beacon-
fuzz [35] is a structure-aware differential fuzzer that generates
BeaconState and BeaconBlock pairs and compares the outcomes of
the Ethereum consensus clients. Fluffy [38] targets the execution
layer, mutating transaction order and semantics to expose diver-
gences across execution clients. Forky [25] constructs valid fork
scenarios to stress the fork-resolution logic. Loki [28] captures live

node states and mutates them via type-specific rules to explore
high-dimensional input spaces. All four treat clients as black boxes
and select mutation targets without referring to the specification’s
validity conditions, so they cannot identify which semantic bound-
aries remain untested.
Differential Testing beyond Blockchain. Differential testing
of multiple implementations conforming to a shared specification
has been applied to JVMs [11, 12], SSL/TLS libraries [13], EVM
bytecode interpreters [22], and Wasm runtimes [41]. These tools
generate inputs via syntactic mutation or code-coverage guidance.
Our mechanized specification instead exposes validity conditions
that the client’s branching structure does not express, so code-level
coverage cannot detect them (§7.2).
Formal Verification of Consensus Protocols. Gasper [8] has
been verified for finality using Coq [6], and model-checking ap-
proaches have targeted individual Beacon Chain components such
as validator exits [33] and reward mechanisms [34]. These efforts
prove properties over abstract models but do not test production
code. Our framework is complementary, targeting implementation-
level conformance across five clients.
9 Conclusion
We present SpecTrum, a specification-guided differential testing
frameworkfor Ethereum consensus clients. By mechanizing thecon-
sensus specification into explicit if-premises, defining premise cov-
erage over them, and generating tests that target under-exercised
conditions, SpecTrum improves the premise coverage of falsifiable
premises from 46.3% of the official test suite to 91.1%. Applied to
five major clients, it exposes 27 cross-client divergence cases, in-
cluding consensus failures caused by lossy uint64 decoding and
client crashes on empty inputs. All 27 cases reproduce across fork
versions, and extending the mechanized specification to a new fork
requires effort proportional to the specification difference. These
results show that cross-client divergences are most likely to arise
at validity boundaries that consensus-spec leaves implicit and the
spectests fail to systematically exercise.
